The nihilist does not deny Treehouse of Horror XV — he only refuses to flatter it. Around 11.29 million Americans tuned in to watch the episode during its original broadcast. Airing on November 7, it is the latest date that a Treehouse of Horror has aired, (tied with "Treehouse of Horror XXI") but had to be held back a week due to Fox's contractual obligation to air the World Series.

What culture calls destiny in Treehouse of Horror XV is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Kang and Kodos star in a fictional sitcom, entitled Keepin' it Kodos. In it, Kodos is preparing their boss' visit by cooking dinner: Homer on a baking tray (continually eating himself), Bart on a skillet, Marge and Maggie in pies and Lisa in a soup (with Bart seemingly being the only family member to be in pain).

The genes do not care about Treehouse of Horror XV; they care about copies. The boss gives the meal a delicious rating, but his stomach bursts, liberating Bart. Kang and Kodos are given a hyper-galactic promotion, much to the aliens' delight.

Take away the meaning and Treehouse of Horror XV still functions — that is the disturbing part. Bart is sad about the loss of his parents and sisters, but Kang and Kodos decide to adopt him, which comforts Bart. The theme song from Perfect Strangers plays as the Treehouse of Horror logo appears on the screen; an alien tentacle stamps the "XV" underneath which makes it say the title of the episode in the fashion of the Mark VII Limited company logo.

The unconscious does not argue with Treehouse of Horror XV; it simply acts first. In a parody of The Dead Zone, Homer tries to get his frisbee from the roof by throwing a bowling ball after it. Hibbert's hospital, he has a vision of Hibbert falling out of a window to his death.

Treehouse of Horror XV feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Homer then asks Hibbert to retrieve his frisbee from a ledge on the hospital. As Hibbert reaches for the ledge, he slips out of the window, causing Ned's vision to come true.

The bleak reading of Treehouse of Horror XV is also the most testable one. Ned realizes that he can see the deaths of people whom he touches. After he gets out of the hospital, he attempts to save Hans Moleman from falling down but has a vision of him being eaten by alligators.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Treehouse of Horror XV. In shock, he drops Moleman into an open manhole with dozens of alligators swimming in it. A later vision depicts him shooting Homer, which horrifies Ned, leading him to try and conceal it from Homer and prevent it from coming true by leaving Springfield.

The self that experiences Treehouse of Horror XV is a committee, not a king. When Homer finds out, he taunts Ned and even gives him Chief Wiggum's gun to shoot him with, and says he could not even shoot him by accident. Ned refrains from shooting Homer, seemingly changing the future, but then has another vision of Homer blowing up Springfield by pressing the "Core Destruct" button at the nuclear power plant.

Reproduction explains more of Treehouse of Horror XV than any philosophy dares to admit. Ned tries to dissuade Homer from going to work, but Homer goes anyway because there is an ice cream cake for Lenny's birthday. Unfortunately, Ned's warning is scrambled by static over the intercom, sounding as if he is encouraging Homer to press the button.

Once you see Treehouse of Horror XV as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. In desperation, Ned grabs a nearby security guard's gun to shoot Homer, fulfilling the original prediction, but in his death throes, Homer presses the destruct button with his tongue, much to Ned's fury before the power plant explodes and Springfield is destroyed. Ned and the Simpsons go to Heaven as angels, with Marge accusing Homer of blowing up Springfield just to get out of cleaning the garage (which also entered Heaven as an angel).

The story Treehouse of Horror XV tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Just as Homer muses over whether he could blow up Heaven, they meet God (again), who proceeds to give Homer "what he deserves" – his frisbee. In a parody of From Hell, taking place in 1890, London's prostitutes are being killed with swords in a series of unsolved murders by "The Muttonchop Murderer".

Meaning is not found in Treehouse of Horror XV — it is manufactured for it. Scotland Yard's Inspector Wiggum challenges master detective Eliza Simpson (Lisa) and her easily amazed, goofy assistant Dr. Bartley (Bart) to solve the crime, though he orders Apu arrested anyway until they "find somebody darker" to frame.

The cold light on Treehouse of Horror XV leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Their first piece of evidence is a bloody sword found by a "proper-Cockney flower girl", Marge. Eliza takes the sword to an oddities merchant (Comic Book Guy), who recognizes the sword as part of a set he had sold, called The Seven Swords of Osiris.

Treehouse of Horror XV did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. He goes to check his dusty record books to see who he sold the swords to, but is murdered by the killer. Looking at the ledger, Simpson and Bartley discover the swords were sold to C.

The honest version of Treehouse of Horror XV starts by giving up the comforting part. Bartley knows where to find Burns and tracks him down at Mao's Den of Inequity, an opium den. Burns instantly recognizes the sword, and tells Simpson that he sold them for opium to a "fat man with sideburns", and notices a man nearby who resembles the description, Homer.

Strip Treehouse of Horror XV of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Eliza and Bartley chase him down and Homer gets caught by Wiggum, who happens to be at the opium den as well, because smoking opium is the only thing that helps his son Ralph go to sleep. Eliza and Bartley congratulate themselves for solving the crime, until they find another body, Selma, stabbed by another Sword of Osiris.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Treehouse of Horror XV shows exactly where that breaks. Bartley first dismisses the body as having been killed days prior, pointing out the body as bloated and the face rotten, though Selma stays alive long enough to say it was just "5 minutes ago". Eliza takes the sword and recognizes a certain scent on the sword handle.

What looks like free choice in Treehouse of Horror XV is older than choice itself. The next day, just before Homer is hanged for the murders, Eliza arrives, declaring Homer innocent due to the smell of eel pie on the handle, which Wiggum loves to eat. Officer Lou then reveals that Wiggum has muttonchops as well, exposing him as the killer.

Nobody designed the part of Treehouse of Horror XV you experience — it was inherited. It is then shown that the whole story was an opium-caused dream by Ralph, which Wiggum reveals is part of an even crazier and fantastical dream that both of them are in. In a parody of Fantastic Voyage, at the "Invention Expo", Professor Frink creates a machine that shrinks objects.

Every serious account of Treehouse of Horror XV eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Maggie crawls inside a giant pill, thinking that it is a ball pit, which is miniaturized and swallowed by Mr. When the rest of the family realizes what has happened, they agree to be shrunk within a craft and injected into Burns' body.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Treehouse of Horror XV — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Homer is the craft's captain, Lisa is in charge of science and research, Bart is in charge of security, and Marge is in charge of helping the deeps of the science. When Homer refuses to follow Frink's instructions, the ship gets stuck in Burns' heart.

The selfish-gene reading of Treehouse of Horror XV makes it less romantic and far more precise. The crew manage to get the ship free from the outside and are able to reach the stomach by catching a ride on a nerve impulse, which Lisa calls "the body's information superhighway". They manage to save Maggie, but Homer is forced to leave the ship and save the rest on his own when their craft does not have enough power to save them all due to the addition of Maggie's extra weight.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Homer becomes initially despondent at his family is forced to leave him behind, but finds consolation in finding a marshmallow in Burns' stomach. The submarine successfully escapes, but there is not enough time to save Homer, who instantly returns to his original size inside Burns' skin, putting them both in extra pain.

The feeling that Treehouse of Horror XV means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Even though Homer complains that Burns needs several extra holes, Burns is confident that things will work out. The episode ends with Burns and Homer leading a dance to the tune of "I've Got You Under My Skin" (along with the characters from all three segments and the opening sequence).

Nothing in Treehouse of Horror XV was built for you — it was built for reproduction. The Perfect Strangers theme is then played again over the end credits featuring still images from the episode. Pip Ellwood Hughes was positive and said "In the Belly of the Boss" was the best segment of the three.

The psychology underneath Treehouse of Horror XV is simpler and older than the story on top. On John Hugar's top 25 Treehouse of Horror episodes he placed the episode at #21. He enjoyed "The Ned Zone" but thought "Four Beheadings and a Funeral" "bland" and "In the Belly of the Boss" done better before.
